GT_Foundations.inherited: From ML_Synthesis: Graph theory will give us another representation of relations. Instead of asking how far points lie from a centre, we will ask which points are connected and what those connections permit.
GT_Foundations.question: Does a graph already contain the order in which we should visit it?
GT_Foundations.ontology: A graph separates vertices from their connections. A traversal adds an order ofvisiting to that relation.
GT_Foundations.experiment: Choose one of the15lamps. Watch the blue tide and then the amber diver reach it; predict which neighbouringlamp lights next.
GT_Foundations.observe: The tide lights successivelevels; the diver follows a branch before returning to another. The same lamps and edges remainthroughout.
GT_Foundations.limit: A drawnheight is not inherent importance, and traversalorder is not the graph itself. A tree also lacks the cycleambiguities of generalgraphs.
GT_Foundations.variation: Existing: follow a deep lamp rather than the root, making its delay the comparison. Proposed: let thevisitor choose the startingvertex or add a cycle.
GT_Foundations.handoff: The next room lets the drawing itself move. Keep the graph’s connections separate from the positions used to display them.
open_questions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

GT_Layout.inherited: From GT_Foundations: The next room lets the drawing itself move. Keep the graph’s connections separate from the positions used to display them.
GT_Layout.question: Can the picture change while the graph stays the same?
GT_Layout.ontology: A layout assigns spatialpositions to vertices. Adjacency says whichvertices are joined and can remain unchanged throughout that movement.
GT_Layout.experiment: Track one movingvertex and count its links before and after the drawing settles.
GT_Layout.observe: Eightvertices move while the same12connections stretch and turn; the defaultgraph is the cubegraph drawn in aplane.
GT_Layout.limit: Closeness on the page is a layoutresult, not necessarily a directconnection. A neatdrawing does not prove its arrangement uniquely represents the graph.
GT_Layout.variation: Existing: compare what you thought was central before/afterrelaxation. Proposed: expose alternate initialpositions with fixedadjacency, then try a ring or star as anexplicit differentgraph.
GT_Layout.handoff: Pathfinding will change a connection’s availability while a traveller is already moving. This time the route really may need to change.
open_questions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

GT_Pathfinding.inherited: From GT_Layout: Pathfinding will change a connection’s availability while a traveller is already moving. This time the route really may need to change.
GT_Pathfinding.question: What happens to the shortest route when a stone disappears?
GT_Pathfinding.ontology: A route is a sequence ofconnected vertices. Shortest refers to summed edgecost on the currentgraph, not the traveller remembering a line.
GT_Pathfinding.experiment: Follow the spark between riverbanks, press thebutton to sink a stone, and compare the next computedroute. Repeat to see an oldstone return after the queue exceeds3.
GT_Pathfinding.observe: A route stone lowers and becomes unavailable; the spark is replanned immediately. Some removals can yield a NO ROUTE message instead of a detour.
GT_Pathfinding.limit: The spark queries agraph, not actualhuman jumpingability. A drawn stone is not a verified walkablesurface or a promise that every removal has analternatepath.
GT_Pathfinding.variation: Existing: intentionally interrupt the route and treat waiting or disconnection as an outcome. Proposed: permit a slower accessible route objective alongside Euclideandistance.
GT_Pathfinding.handoff: Network analysis asks what the arrangement as a whole makes possible: which vertices connect many others, and which only look important in the drawing?
open_questions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

GT_Network_Analysis.inherited: From GT_Pathfinding: Network analysis asks what the arrangement as a whole makes possible: which vertices connect many others, and which only look important in the drawing?
GT_Network_Analysis.question: Is the biggest node the one whose connections matter most?
GT_Network_Analysis.ontology: Degree counts immediateconnections; othercentrality measures answer different questions about routes or influence. Drawing a hub is distinct from measuring one.
GT_Network_Analysis.experiment: Choose one largenode and one smallnode. Count their visibleconnections and trace at least one route through each before trusting its visualrank.
GT_Network_Analysis.observe: The scene stages5central,8middle and12peripheral nodes, connecting and animating them with deliberately different sizes andcolours.
GT_Network_Analysis.limit: This is a networkdiagram, not a validatedcentrality calculator. Sizeandcolour may guide a hypothesis but cannot serve as evidence that its assignedtier isimportant.
GT_Network_Analysis.variation: Existing: begin from a peripheralnode and identify what its routespermit. Proposed: compute and show actual degree orbetweenness, then compare with the originalvisual hierarchy.
GT_Network_Analysis.handoff: Connectivity next gives us one exact question to test: where can a directed traveller go and still return?
open_questions: Centrality values and summary animation are not calculated from the displayed edges. Compute one named measure and let the visitor check its supporting connections.
Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Central concept gap: calculatecentrality from adjacency before treating visualhierarchy asalgorithmic result.

GT_Connectivity.inherited: From GT_Network_Analysis: Connectivity next gives us one exact question to test: where can a directed traveller go and still return?
GT_Connectivity.question: If you can reach another node, can you get back?
GT_Connectivity.ontology: A strongly connectedcomponent is a maximal set whosevertices can reach eachother along directedpaths. One-way contact is insufficient.
GT_Connectivity.experiment: Pick two vertices joined by anarrow, then trace a returnroute. Watch the automaticsearch assign componentcolours and compare its grouping with your prediction.
GT_Connectivity.observe: Current, visited, backedge andcomponent colours expose a depth-firstsearch; the status announces each discoveredcomponent.
GT_Connectivity.limit: Mutualreachability is a precise relation in this directedgraph, not mutualtrust, equality or universalaccess. A one-way bridge can connect a drawing without merging its strongcomponents.
GT_Connectivity.variation: Existing: search for a route that leaves acomponent and cannot return. Proposed: expose a reversiblearrow and observe whichcomponents merge.
GT_Connectivity.handoff: Spanning trees will ask how many connections can be removed while everyone remains connected. The useful return route you just found may look like an expendable cycle under a different objective.
open_questions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

GT_Spanning_Trees.inherited: From GT_Connectivity: Spanning trees will ask how many connections can be removed while everyone remains connected. The useful return route you just found may look like an expendable cycle under a different objective.
GT_Spanning_Trees.question: Which connections can be removed while keeping everyone connected?
GT_Spanning_Trees.ontology: A spanningtree connects everyvertex withoutcycles. A minimumspanningtree minimizes totaledgeweight among suchtrees for a connectedweighted undirectedgraph.
GT_Spanning_Trees.experiment: Watch candidateedges receive attention and greenedges join thebackbone. Before eachdecision, predict whether accepting theedge would close acycle.
GT_Spanning_Trees.observe: Acceptededges accumulate until the backboneconnects allvertices; some edges are skipped even when short because their ends already belong to thesamecomponent.
GT_Spanning_Trees.limit: Lowesttotalcost does not provide redundantconnections. Every treeedge is a singlepoint of disconnection if removed; reliability may justify an extraedge.
GT_Spanning_Trees.variation: Existing: mentally remove an acceptededge and identify the two resultinggroups. Proposed: compare the cheapesttree with a deliberately redundantnetwork and name the extracost.
GT_Spanning_Trees.handoff: Flow adds another constraint. A route may exist and still be unable to carry everything trying to pass through it.
open_questions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

GT_Flow.inherited: From GT_Spanning_Trees: Flow adds another constraint. A route may exist and still be unable to carry everything trying to pass through it.
GT_Flow.question: When a junction receives more than it can send onward, where does the excess go?
GT_Flow.ontology: Capacity limits anedge; flow is the currentallocation; excess is netmaterial held temporarily at anintermediatevertex. Height is analgorithmiclabel used to routeupdates.
GT_Flow.experiment: Follow the sourceoutflow, then watch a junction with excess and read its PUSH orRELABEL status.
GT_Flow.observe: Sourceedges fill first; a vertex may pass availableflow to a lowerheight neighbour or change itsheight when itcannotpush. Pervertexheight/excess and overallflow labels are drawn.
GT_Flow.limit: A full maximumflow solver needs residualreverse edges so earlierallocations can be undone. This implementation does not maintain them and cannot support its blanket maximumclaim.
GT_Flow.variation: Proposed nextbuild: draw reversible residualcapacity and let visitors inspect a rerouting case; meanwhile compare a localpush to the sinktotal without assuming everylocaldecision isfinal.
GT_Flow.handoff: Matching will impose a different limit: each vertex may have only one selected partner. Once again, an early acceptable choice may need to be undone.
open_questions: The current flow procedure lacks reverse residual adjustments. Add a case requiring rerouting and implement the complete algorithm before claiming maximum flow.

GT_Matching.inherited: From GT_Flow: Matching will impose a different limit: each vertex may have only one selected partner. Once again, an early acceptable choice may need to be undone.
GT_Matching.question: Can an early pairing prevent a larger set of pairings later?
GT_Matching.ontology: A matching is a set ofedges with no sharedendpoint. A maximalmatching cannot add anotheredge; a maximummatching has the largestpossible number ofedges. These are differentclaims.
GT_Matching.experiment: Watch the next highlightededge. Predict acceptance by checking whether bothendpoints are still unmatched; track onevertex leftwithout a partner.
GT_Matching.observe: Edgesare scanned in their storedorder. When bothendpoints are free they become a pair, and neither is reconsideredlater.
GT_Matching.limit: A completegreedy scan gives a maximalmatching, not necessarilymaximum. On a fourvertexpath, choosing the middleedge first leavesone pair where choosing bothouteredges would giv two.
GT_Matching.variation: Proposed: expose edgeorder or a4vertexpath counterexample, then add augmentingpath updates. Existing: identify which earlierpair blocks a latercandidate.
GT_Matching.handoff: The foundations sequence will question what a formal system can establish. Carry one distinction forward: a procedure meeting its local rule is not automatically a proof of its strongest advertised conclusion.
open_questions: The Edmonds-labelled display performs a greedy scan. Add augmenting-path behaviour and the four-vertex path counterexample before claiming a maximum matching.
